The Greek word in Matthew 24:14 is oikoumene, the inhabited world of the Roman Empire. Luke uses the same word for Augustus' census of "all the world" (Luke 2:1) and for the famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28). Paul writes that the gospel had already been heard in all the world and preached to every creature under heaven (Romans 1:8; Colossians 1:6, 1:23). So this reading holds that the condition was met before the end came in AD 70.

This reading answers that "coming on the clouds" is the Old Testament language of God coming in judgment, as against Egypt, where no one saw a body in the sky. Jesus told the high priest that he would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds, which this reading takes as seeing His judgment in history. Partial preterists add that Matthew 24 describes a coming in judgment in AD 70, but they still expect a future, bodily Second Coming. Full preterists hold that the one promised coming took place in AD 70.

This reading never makes light of later horrors such as the Holocaust. It notes that "never before or after" is a set phrase that Scripture uses for several different events (Exodus 11:6; Ezekiel 5:9; Daniel 9:12; Joel 2:2), so it measures weight rather than counting deaths. AD 70 was unique in covenant meaning: the end of the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices. Josephus himself wrote that the misfortunes of all nations since the world began were small compared with those of the Jews in that war (Josephus, Jewish War, Preface 4).

Fulfilled readers answer in two ways. Some link the "times of the Gentiles" to the forty-two months in which the nations trample the holy city (Revelation 11:2), so the phrase describes the war itself. Others accept that Gentile rule over Jerusalem lasted long after AD 70, but note that Luke 21:24 describes what follows the fall of the city. Jesus' time limit (Luke 21:32) covers the things the disciples asked about, which centred on the temple's destruction. Partial preterists often take this second view.

Here preterists differ. Partial preterists agree that Acts 1:11 promises a future, bodily, visible return, distinct from the coming in judgment in AD 70. Full preterists answer that "in like manner" points to the manner, not to who would see it: He left in a cloud, seen only by His disciples, and He would come in the cloud of God's glory and judgment. Most churches through history have read Acts 1:11 as a future bodily return.

Some early writers did connect much of the discourse with AD 70. Eusebius quoted Jesus' warnings (Matthew 24:19-21) and set them beside Josephus' account of the siege, saying the prophecy was fulfilled (Eusebius, Church History 3.7.1-2). Others, such as John Chrysostom, read the great tribulation in the same way. Yet the same writers also expected a future return of Christ, a bodily resurrection and a final judgment, as the creeds confess. Partial preterists see this as support for their view, while full preterists hold that the fathers did not fully see the time texts.

This is the main point where fulfilled readers divide. Full preterists tie the resurrection of Daniel 12:2 to the time when the power of the holy people is shattered (Daniel 12:7), and they read it as a corporate, covenant resurrection completed in AD 70. Partial preterists, with nearly all churches through history, hold that the bodily resurrection and the final judgment are still future. They note that Paul warned against those who said the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:17-18). This study presents the full-preterist answer as one view, not the view of the church as a whole.

This reading notes that the Greek word genea means people living at the same time, while a different word, genos, means a race or kind. Every other use of "this generation" in Matthew refers to Jesus' own hearers (Matthew 11:16; 12:41-45; 23:36). In Matthew 23:36 Jesus says that all the judgment He has just described will come on "this generation", only verses before the discourse begins. Jesus also said that some standing there would not die before seeing Him come in His kingdom (Matthew 16:28).

The fulfilled reading of Matthew 24 does not depend on the date of Revelation, because Jesus spoke around AD 30 and set the limit of "this generation". On Revelation itself, many fulfilled readers argue for a date in the 60s from evidence inside the book, such as the measured temple and the sixth king (see the Revelation dating section). They also note that the key line in Irenaeus can be read in more than one way (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3). Many scholars still hold the later date.

This reading answers that Jesus gave one time limit for "all these things" (Matthew 24:34). He also said the great tribulation would be unlike anything before it or after it (Matthew 24:21), which would rule out a greater repeat. Daniel was told to seal his book because its time was far away, but John was told not to seal his because the time was near (Daniel 12:4; Revelation 22:10). Some partial preterists do see AD 70 as a pattern or preview of the final coming, while full preterists reject any second fulfilment.

Matthew 16:27-28 says Jesus would come in his Father's glory with his angels and repay each person for what they had done, and that only some of those present would live to see it. At the transfiguration all were alive, no angels came and no one was judged, and Jesus called it a vision. Pentecost fails on the same points. The fall of Jerusalem about forty years later, when James and Peter had died but John lived, fits every detail. Many read the transfiguration as a preview of that coming.

Paul defines Israel himself: not all descended from Israel are Israel (Romans 9:6-8). He saw a remnant chosen by grace in his own day (11:5) and Gentiles grafted into the same olive tree. He then says “in this way” (houtōs), not “after this”, all Israel will be saved. Romans 11 mentions no temple, sacrifices or throne. Some who share this reading still expect many Jewish people to turn to Christ, grafted into the same tree.

Revelation says it was “signified”, shown in signs (1:1). Scripture uses “thousand” for fullness: God owns the cattle on a thousand hills and keeps covenant to a thousand generations (Psalm 50:10; Deuteronomy 7:9). Partial preterists and postmillennialists read the thousand years as the long, complete reign of Christ that began at his ascension and still continues.

Jesus called the siege of Jerusalem the days of vengeance, “that all things which are written may be fulfilled”. In context these are the things written about the judgement of Jerusalem, from the Song of Moses to Daniel. Partial preterists do not stretch the verse further, because Scripture still promises Christ's bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgement (Acts 1:11; 1 Corinthians 15:23-28), as the creeds confess.

Most covenant readers agree. Partial preterists and many full preterists read Genesis 1 as the real creation and use covenant meaning only for later prophetic texts. The minority that reads Genesis 1 covenantally answers that the Sabbath was itself a covenant sign (Exodus 31:13-17) and that Israel's tabernacle was built in a creation pattern. Yet Exodus 20:11 lists sea and every creature, so the physical sense is hard to remove there.

The covenantal reading notes that ktisis can mean people (Mark 16:15; Colossians 1:23), and that 'earnest expectation' and 'groaning' fit people waiting for God's sons. Others in this reading accept that the physical creation is meant and say its freedom comes as God's sons are revealed, a process begun in Christ. Partial preterists keep a future bodily resurrection (8:23) and so keep a future renewal; full preterists place the 'revealing' in the first century.

Peter ties the restoration to what 'all the prophets' said and adds that they 'foretold of these days' (3:24). The covenantal reading sees restoration of Israel's remnant and the blessing of the nations through Abraham's seed (3:25-26), in progress since Pentecost. Partial preterists usually add that the restoration is completed at Christ's final coming; full preterists say it was completed by AD 70.

Partial preterists agree: they apply Matthew 24:35 and much of 2 Peter 3 to AD 70 but hold a future bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:23-26; John 5:28-29) and so a renewed creation at the end. Full preterists answer that the resurrection of 1 Corinthians 15 is the raising of God's people from the death of Adam into new covenant life, fulfilled in the first century. This is the main point where the two covenant readings divide.

The covenantal reading agrees that Psalm 148 speaks of real creatures, and it does not claim that every heaven-and-earth text is a symbol. Its point is narrower: some texts, like Isaiah 49:13 or Psalm 69:34-35, tie the praise of heaven and earth to the saving of Zion. Context decides. Psalm 148 also ends with the people 'near unto him' (148:14), so creation and covenant are joined.

If it means 'never', the whole law, including temple sacrifice and food laws, would still bind today, which Hebrews 8:13 and Mark 7:19 deny. The covenantal reading says the law stood until its fulfilment ('till all be fulfilled'), and the old covenant world passed with the temple in AD 70. Others reply that Christ fulfilled the law at the cross and that its moral core lasts as long as the world.

On Matthew 24:35 and 2 Peter 3 the covenantal reading has older support: John Lightfoot, John Owen (on 2 Peter 3) and John Brown (on Matthew 5:18) applied the passing of heaven and earth to the Jewish order in AD 70. Partial preterists affirm the creeds fully, since they keep a future return, resurrection and judgment. Full preterists admit they differ from the creeds and appeal to Scripture as the final authority, a point other Christians find serious.

Full preterists read 'death' here as the covenant death that came through sin and the law (Romans 7:9-11; 1 Corinthians 15:56), removed for those in Christ; physical death remains but has lost its sting. Partial preterists usually say Revelation 21-22 is the final state, or that it describes the church now and its full future form. Isaiah 65:20, with death at a hundred years, shows the 'new heavens' can contain physical death.

The covenantal reading notes that the flood destroyed the 'world' of ungodly people (2 Peter 2:5), yet the planet survived. In the same way the fire judges 'ungodly men' (3:7), which was fulfilled when Jerusalem burned in AD 70. Others reply that the flood was a real event on the real earth, so the coming fire is a real, final judgment.

The word can mean physical elements, letters of an alphabet, or basic rules. Paul uses it for old covenant rules (Galatians 4:3, 9; Colossians 2:8, 20; Hebrews 5:12 'first principles'). The covenantal reading takes this sense for Peter, who writes to Jewish believers in the last days of the temple. Others note Peter speaks of 'heavens' first, so heavenly bodies are a natural meaning.

Most covenant readers say 'first' means the former covenant order, as Hebrews calls the old covenant the 'first' (8:7, 13; 9:1). The minority view goes further and links 'first' to Genesis 1, reading the whole creation account as covenantal. Others answer that Genesis 1 is plainly the original creation, so a renewed physical world is in view.

The covenantal reading says 'that day' simply means a day still future to the speaker, as 'this' marks what is near. Verse 35 confirms the whole prophecy, and the Noah comparison (24:37-41) still fits Jerusalem's sudden fall. Many partial preterists (and earlier commentators like Charles Spurgeon) see a transition here to the second coming; this is a real debate among partial preterists themselves.

Jesus stops reading before “the day of vengeance.” But Isaiah 61 has no numbered count; Daniel 9 counts seventy weeks and says what happens after the 62nd. A pause in reading is not a gap in a count. And the day of vengeance came within that generation (Luke 21:22).

Daniel 9:26 places the destruction “after the sixty-two weeks” without saying it falls inside the seventy. The seventy weeks decree the Messiah's work; the desolation is its consequence, “determined” for the people who rejected him. Jesus gave that generation forty years to repent.

Grammatically, “prince” is in a dependent phrase (“the people of the prince”). The main figure of the passage is the Anointed One. Many Hebrew scholars, ancient and modern, take the Messiah as the subject of 9:27, and the covenant language fits him.
Yes, future in AD 30, and he told his hearers to flee when they saw it. Luke explains it as Jerusalem surrounded by armies. It came in AD 66-70.

He announced it: “the time is fulfilled” (Mark 1:15). Luke reports that the people were in expectation of the Messiah in John's day (Luke 3:15), and Jewish writers of the period expected a deliverer around then.

Luke dates John's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, which most place in AD 28-29, with some counting from his co-regency in AD 26-27. Jesus was about thirty. The fit is within a year or two, remarkable for a prophecy given five centuries earlier.
When Paul wrote, around AD 51, the temple stood, and he said the lawlessness was already at work and the readers knew the restrainer. A first-century fulfilment fits his words.

Revelation is a book of signs (1:1). Its numbers are symbolic throughout: seven spirits, 144,000, twelve gates. A thousand years pictures a long, complete reign. Partial preterists still expect a future final judgement after it.
Paul says so: it was proclaimed in all creation under heaven and bearing fruit in the whole world. The word for world in Matthew 24:14 is the inhabited earth, the Roman world, as in Luke 2:1.

Its picture of nations gathered against Jerusalem and half the city exiled fits AD 70, and its living waters and the LORD as king over all the earth are applied to the gospel age (John 7:38). Some partial preterists also see final elements in it.
No. Partial preterists confess the bodily return and look for it. What they reject is the expectation of a seven-year tribulation, a rebuilt temple and an Antichrist treaty drawn from Daniel 9.

Daniel 8 is explicitly about Greece (8:21) and its numbers fit 171-164 BC. Daniel 9 is about the Anointed One being cut off and the city and sanctuary destroyed, which Antiochus did not do: he defiled the temple but did not destroy it.

That date rests mainly on a sentence in Irenaeus that can be read as saying John was seen, not the vision, in Domitian's time. Revelation itself shows the temple standing (11:1-2) and the sixth king reigning (17:10), and never mentions the fall of Jerusalem, which would have been a powerful example. Many scholars hold an early date of about AD 65-68.

The word often translated “earth” also means “land,” as when “all the tribes of the land” mourn over the one they pierced (1:7; Zechariah 12:10-12). The prophets used cosmic language for the fall of Babylon, Egypt and Edom (Isaiah 13; 34; Ezekiel 32).

The beast she rides is Rome on its seven hills; the harlot is carried by it, as Jerusalem's leaders allied with Rome against Christ (“We have no king but Caesar,” John 19:15). Some partial preterists do read the harlot as Rome itself.
The same refusal is said of the land's people throughout Jesus' ministry (Matthew 11:20-24). The judgements fall on those who chose the beast, while the sealed servants are protected.

Some matches are closer than others, and partial preterists should hold them loosely. But the overall pattern of war, famine, factional slaughter, the temple burned and the city split into three is well documented, and the main point does not depend on any single detail.

No. Partial preterists read some “comings” in Revelation as Christ coming in judgement on that generation, as the prophets spoke of the LORD coming on the clouds against Egypt (Isaiah 19:1). They confess his future bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgement.

It says “even those who pierced him” and “all the tribes of the land,” quoting Zechariah 12 about Jerusalem's mourning. Jesus told the high priest he would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds (Matthew 26:64).

Revelation moves from the judgement on the old order to the reign of Christ, the final rebellion and the last judgement, and the new creation. Partial preterists see the thousand-year reign as now, and the great white throne and full new creation as still to come.

No. Jesus said all who are in the tombs will come out (John 5:28-29); God has fixed a day to judge the world (Acts 17:31); it is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgement (Hebrews 9:27). Reading some warnings historically leaves these untouched.

No. Christians hold different views of final punishment: conscious punishment, final destruction, and others. This study shows only that many Gehenna sayings first pointed to Jerusalem's judgement. Matthew 10:28 is the strongest text for a wider meaning, and it is noted honestly.

That picture comes from a medieval commentator (around 1200) and is not in ancient sources. What Scripture and history show is Hinnom as a place of idolatry and, in Jeremiah, of the slaughtered dead. Josephus says the siege dead were thrown into “the valleys” without naming Hinnom.
Unlikely. In John 3:16 perishing is set against eternal life, and John's Gospel uses “eternal life” for life with God now and beyond death. This study does not adopt that reading.
Some suggest it from Hebrews 12:1, but in Matthew 24:30 the clouds are the prophets' judgement imagery (Isaiah 19:1). Partial preterists also keep the visible bodily return of Acts 1:11 future.
Eusebius gives no numbers; he says the church was warned before the war and moved to Pella. Some historians question the account. Larger claims about numbers go beyond the evidence.
